BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Thousands of people marched in central Baghdad on Saturday to protest a proposed U.S.-Iraqi security agreement that would extend the presence of U.S. troops in the country after the end of the year. Thousands staged a mass march through Baghdad, Iraq, on Saturday to protest a planned U.S.-Iraq security deal. The political party of Iraqi cleric Muqtada al-Sadr called for the rally. At one point, several speakers at a podium addressed the mass of people, urging the Iraqi government to reject the proposal. "End the U.S. occupation of Iraq!" one speaker shouted in English. Hazem al-Araji, a senior al-Sadr aide, told protesters their voices would be heard in America. "Thanks to you, to these voices and the millions of voices, George Bush will hear these millions of calls in his 'Black House' -- in which you shouted out, 'No, no, America!'" he said.  Watch protesters wave flags, swarm street » . "This talk and these words are that of the leader, Muqtada al-Sadr: Baghdad is free, free! America, get out. This voice does not reach the Green Zone. We want to hear everyone who is occupied in that area saying Baghdad is free, free, America get out!" al-Araji exclaimed. Protesters clogged several streets in the capital, waving Iraqi flags and kicking up dust. The demonstration, the largest in Baghdad in several months, was largely peaceful. Pentagon spokesman Geoff Morrell said in Washington on Thursday a draft status-of-forces agreement authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq had "been agreed upon by U.S. and Iraqi negotiators" and was being reviewed by the two governments. A U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. troop presence in Iraq expires December 31, and U.S. officials are examining "contingencies" in case the Iraqi government is unable to sell the status-of-forces deal to the country's various factions, a senior Bush administration official said this week. The same official said negotiations on the pact had finished and the text was final. The official said the "final" draft calls for U.S. troops to be out of Iraqi cities by June 2009 and out of Iraq by the end of 2011 unless the Iraqis ask the United States to stay. The U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions, said negotiators had also "reached a compromise" on the issue of U.S. troops remaining immune from Iraqi law -- an issue that was a major hurdle in the talks. Baghdad has sought the power to arrest and try Americans accused of crimes not related to official military operations, plus jurisdiction over troops and contractors who commit grave mistakes in the course of their duties. The United States has insisted its troops and contractors remain immune from Iraqi law. CNN State Department Producer Elise Labott contributed to this report.

The demonstration, which stretched across several major thoroughfares in the heart of the capital, was the largest to take place in Baghdad in months. Waving Iraqi flags and hoisting banners denouncing the continued foreign military presence, marchers chanted slogans demanding a firm timetable for the withdrawal of U.S. forces. Many carried portraits of al-Sadr, whose Mahdi Army had clashed repeatedly with American troops in the years following the 2003 invasion, and whose movement remains a powerful voice among Iraq's Shiite population.

Despite the size and intensity of the crowd, the protest remained largely peaceful. Iraqi security forces were deployed in significant numbers along the route to prevent any outbreak of violence, but the rally proceeded without major incident. Organizers framed the event as a show of national sovereignty, arguing that Iraq should not commit to any arrangement that would prolong what they described as an occupation.

The rally came at a critical moment in negotiations between Washington and Baghdad. U.S. and Iraqi officials have been working to finalize a draft status-of-forces agreement, which would set out the legal framework governing the presence and conduct of American troops in the country. That draft is now under review by the Iraqi government, where it faces scrutiny from lawmakers and political factions deeply divided over how long, and under what conditions, foreign forces should remain.

Adding urgency to the talks is the looming expiration of the United Nations mandate that has authorized the deployment of American and coalition troops in Iraq. That mandate is set to lapse on December 31, and without either a renewal or a bilateral agreement in its place, the legal basis for the continued American military presence would be thrown into question. Negotiators on both sides have been racing to reach terms before the deadline, even as popular movements like al-Sadr's press their case in the streets.

The scale of Saturday's turnout underscored the political challenge facing Iraqi leaders as they weigh the security agreement. While the government has cited ongoing instability and the need to build up Iraqi forces as reasons to maintain American support, opposition figures and their supporters have argued that the deal risks compromising the nation's independence. The competing pressures leave officials to balance strategic considerations against a wave of public sentiment demanding an end to the foreign military footprint.

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of demonstrators flooded into central Baghdad on Friday to protest a proposed security agreement between the United States and Iraq, answering a call from followers of anti-American Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr who denounced the deal as an assault on Iraqi sovereignty.

The crowds, many waving Iraqi flags and chanting "No, no to America," gathered after Friday prayers in a show of force that underscored the deep divisions surrounding the negotiations over the future of American troops in the country.

## Sadr Movement Voices Opposition

Aides to al-Sadr framed the protest as a rejection of any long-term U.S. military presence.

"This agreement represents the continuation of the occupation under a different name," said one senior al-Sadr aide who addressed the crowd. "The Iraqi people did not sacrifice their blood to hand over their sovereignty to foreign powers."

Another representative of the movement told reporters that the cleric's followers would continue to press their case through peaceful demonstrations. "We reject any deal that keeps American soldiers on our soil and grants them immunity from our laws," he said. "The voice of the street cannot be ignored."

Al-Sadr, who commands a substantial following among Iraq's Shiite majority and whose Mahdi Army militia clashed repeatedly with U.S. forces, has emerged as one of the most vocal opponents of the agreement.

## Status-of-Forces Negotiations

The proposed accord, known as a status-of-forces agreement, would establish the legal framework governing the presence of American troops in Iraq after the United Nations mandate authorizing the multinational force expires at the end of the year.

Negotiators from both governments have been wrestling with several contentious issues, including the timeline for a U.S. withdrawal, whether American troops and contractors would be subject to Iraqi law, and the extent to which U.S. forces could conduct operations without Iraqi approval.

Iraqi officials have pushed for firm timelines tied to conditions on the ground, while some lawmakers have demanded greater guarantees of national sovereignty before any agreement is brought before parliament for ratification.

U.S. officials have said the agreement is intended to provide a stable legal foundation for continued cooperation as Iraqi security forces assume greater responsibility for the country's security.

## A Test for the Government

The demonstration presented a challenge for Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government, which must balance domestic political pressures against the practical realities of an ongoing security partnership with Washington.

The scale of Friday's protest highlighted the political risks facing Iraqi leaders as they weigh a deal that critics say could compromise the country's independence, even as violence has declined in recent months.

Whether the agreement can secure the necessary support in Iraq's fractious parliament remains uncertain, with the Sadr movement vowing to mobilize continued opposition in the streets and in the political arena.

# Thousands Rally in Baghdad Against Extended U.S. Troop Presence

**BAGHDAD** — Thousands of demonstrators flooded central Baghdad on Saturday to reject any extension of the U.S. military presence in Iraq, underscoring deep public opposition as officials weigh whether American forces should remain beyond a year-end withdrawal deadline.

Chanting "No, no to America" and "Get out, occupier," protesters gathered in a square in the capital, many waving Iraqi flags and holding banners denouncing what they described as foreign interference in the country's affairs. Organizers said the crowd numbered in the thousands, drawn from across the city and surrounding provinces.

The demonstration reflected a groundswell of nationalist sentiment as the deadline approaches for the roughly remaining U.S. troops to leave under a bilateral security agreement.

"We came out today to send a clear message: the Iraqi people do not want the occupier to stay one more day," said one protester, a schoolteacher who traveled from a nearby district. "We can protect our own country."

## Government Weighs Its Options

The rally comes as Iraqi political leaders remain divided over whether to request that a limited number of U.S. forces stay behind, primarily to continue training Iraqi security forces and provide logistical support.

Supporters of an extension argue that Iraqi troops still lack capabilities in areas such as air defense, intelligence, and border security. Opponents, including powerful political blocs, insist that any prolonged presence would violate Iraqi sovereignty and inflame public anger.

A government spokesman said officials were still consulting with political factions and had reached no final decision. "The question of trainers is a technical matter that must be decided by consensus among Iraq's political leadership," he said, adding that any agreement would respect "the will of the Iraqi people."

A senior lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity because the deliberations are ongoing, said negotiations were "extremely sensitive" and that no bloc wanted to be seen as endorsing a continued American footprint. "Everyone is watching the street," the lawmaker said.

## Background: The Security Agreement

Under the Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) signed in 2008, U.S. combat forces were required to withdraw from Iraqi cities by mid-2009 and to complete a full withdrawal from the country by the end of 2011. The agreement, negotiated after months of difficult talks, was widely seen at the time as a milestone in restoring Iraqi sovereignty following the 2003 invasion.

Any decision to keep American troops in the country beyond the deadline would require a new agreement — and, most likely, fresh parliamentary approval — reopening a politically charged debate over immunity for U.S. personnel and the scope of any residual mission.

U.S. officials have said they are prepared to discuss a continued training relationship if the Iraqi government formally requests one, but have emphasized that the initiative must come from Baghdad.

## A Test of Sovereignty

For many demonstrators, the issue is less about military logistics than national dignity.

"This is about our independence," said a young man who marched with a group of friends. "We have suffered enough. It is time for Iraqis to decide the future of Iraq."

Religious and political leaders opposed to the presence have urged supporters to keep up peaceful pressure through demonstrations, warning that they would resist any extension by "all legitimate means."

Security forces deployed around the rally site but reported no major incidents. Organizers said further demonstrations were planned in the coming weeks as the deadline draws nearer.

*— With reporting from Baghdad.*

# Thousands Rally in Baghdad Against U.S.-Iraq Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Tens of thousands of followers of Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr poured into the streets of Baghdad on Saturday, denouncing a proposed security agreement that would govern the presence of American troops in Iraq, in one of the largest demonstrations of anti-American sentiment the capital has seen this year.

The protesters, many waving Iraqi flags and holding portraits of al-Sadr, gathered in the vast expanse of Firdos Square — the same plaza where U.S. Marines helped topple a statue of Saddam Hussein in the spring of 2003. The symbolism was not lost on the crowd, some of whom trampled and burned American flags as speakers denounced what they called a continuing occupation.

"No, no to America! No, no to the occupier!" the demonstrators chanted, their voices rising across the square under a heavy security presence. Iraqi police and army units, some backed by armored vehicles, ringed the demonstration but did not intervene as the largely peaceful crowd swelled through the morning.

## A Show of Strength

The rally underscored the enduring ability of al-Sadr, whose Mahdi Army militia twice battled American forces, to mobilize his impoverished Shiite base against the pact, formally known as the Status of Forces Agreement. Though the young cleric is believed to be studying in Iran, his movement remains a potent political force with a bloc of seats in Iraq's parliament.

"We reject the agreement that makes Iraq subordinate to the Americans," said Sheikh Salah al-Obeidi, a spokesman for the Sadr movement, addressing the crowd. He called on Iraqis to voice their opposition through peaceful means but warned that the pact would compromise Iraqi sovereignty.

Among the demonstrators, many of whom had traveled from the sprawling Sadr City district and from southern provinces, the grievances were personal as much as political.

"My brother was killed by the Americans. Why should they stay?" said one middle-aged man from Sadr City, who gave his name only as Abu Karrar. "We want them to leave and set a date to go."

## The Agreement in Dispute

The security pact, under negotiation between Washington and Baghdad for months, would provide the legal basis for U.S. forces to remain in Iraq after the United Nations mandate expires at the end of 2008. A draft of the accord calls for American combat troops to withdraw from Iraqi cities by mid-2009 and for a full withdrawal by the end of 2011.

The agreement has become the subject of fierce debate within Iraq's fractious political establishment. While Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government has cautiously backed the framework, subject to amendments, Sadrist lawmakers and some other factions have condemned it. The issue has also become entangled in regional tensions, with neighboring Iran openly critical of any long-term American military footprint.

## Washington Responds

In Washington, administration and Pentagon officials sought to characterize the negotiations as a partnership respecting Iraqi sovereignty rather than an imposition.

A Pentagon spokesman said the draft agreement "reflects the improving security situation and the growing capabilities of Iraqi security forces," adding that the timelines contained in the document were "aspirational goals based on conditions on the ground." Defense officials have repeatedly stressed that any withdrawal would be governed by security realities rather than fixed dates alone.

State Department officials, meanwhile, emphasized that the agreement remained subject to approval by Iraq's parliament. "This is a sovereign decision for the Iraqi government and the Iraqi people to make," a department official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity because the negotiations were ongoing.

The White House framed the protests as evidence of the very democratic freedoms that the American presence had helped to establish. "The fact that Iraqis can gather and express their views freely is a sign of how much the country has changed," a spokesman said.

## An Uncertain Path

For all the emotion on display in Firdos Square, the ultimate fate of the agreement rests with Iraqi lawmakers, who remained deeply divided as the U.N. mandate's expiration loomed. Analysts noted that al-Sadr's ability to fill the streets sent a pointed message to al-Maliki, a fellow Shiite who has increasingly asserted his independence from the Sadrists after launching military operations against their militia earlier in the year.

As the afternoon wore on, the crowds began to disperse peacefully, filing back toward the buses that had brought them. But the demonstration served as a reminder that whatever the diplomats in Baghdad and Washington ultimately agreed upon, a significant portion of the Iraqi public remained unwilling to accept an extended American stay.

"We will not stop," said Abu Karrar, folding his flag as he prepared to leave. "This is our country."

*— With reporting from Baghdad and Washington.*

**Thousands March in Baghdad as U.N. Mandate Nears Expiration, Demanding Faster U.S. Exit**

*BAGHDAD — November 21, 2008* — Tens of thousands of demonstrators poured into Firdos Square and the surrounding streets of central Baghdad on Friday, burning American flags and chanting for an immediate end to the foreign military presence in Iraq, as the U.N. Security Council mandate authorizing coalition forces prepared to lapse at the end of the year.

The protest, called by followers of the Shiite cleric Moqtada al-Sadr, unfolded beneath a heavy Iraqi security presence and reflected the deep public anxiety surrounding the newly negotiated Status of Forces Agreement, or SOFA, which would govern the terms and timeline of the American withdrawal after the U.N. mandate expires on December 31.

Demonstrators gathered at the same square where a statue of Saddam Hussein was toppled in April 2003, an image broadcast worldwide as a symbol of the invasion's early days. On Friday, protesters trampled and set fire to an effigy meant to represent the U.S. occupation, while others held banners reading "No, No to America" and "Yes, Yes to Iraq."

"We reject any agreement that keeps the occupier on our soil for even one more day," said Kadhim al-Fartousi, a 34-year-old schoolteacher from the Sadr City district, who traveled with neighbors to join the rally. "Three years is not a withdrawal. It is a lease."

**A Contested Timeline**

At the heart of the dispute is the security pact hammered out over months of tense negotiation between Baghdad and Washington. The agreement, approved by Iraq's cabinet on Sunday and awaiting a parliamentary vote, calls for American combat forces to pull out of Iraqi cities by June 30, 2009, and for a full U.S. withdrawal from the country by December 31, 2011.

Supporters, including Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government, have described the pact as a milestone that restores Iraqi sovereignty and sets a firm, dated end to a military presence that has lasted more than five years. Critics — chief among them the Sadrist movement — argue that the timeline is too long and that provisions allowing continued American operations amount to a prolonged occupation under a new name.

"This agreement legitimizes the presence of the occupier," Sheikh Salah al-Obeidi, a spokesman for al-Sadr, told reporters at the demonstration. "The Iraqi people did not shed their blood so that foreign soldiers could stay by the stroke of a pen. We want them out, and we want them out now."

The looming expiration of the U.N. mandate has added urgency to the debate. The Security Council authorization, first granted in 2003 and renewed annually, provides the legal basis for the roughly 150,000 American troops still stationed in Iraq. Without either an extension of that mandate — which Iraqi leaders have declined to seek — or ratification of the bilateral agreement, U.S. forces would face a legal vacuum after December 31.

**Political Fault Lines**

The protest laid bare the sectarian and political divisions that continue to shape post-invasion Iraq. The Sadrist bloc, which commands significant support among poor Shiites and holds seats in parliament, has vowed to vote against the pact and has organized a series of Friday demonstrations to pressure lawmakers.

Iraqi government officials sought to project confidence that the agreement would pass. "This is a sovereign decision made in the interest of all Iraqis," said Ali al-Dabbagh, the government spokesman, in remarks to state media. "It ends the mandate, it ends the occupation on a clear schedule, and it gives Iraq control over its own security."

American officials, for their part, have emphasized that the agreement reflects a partnership rather than an imposition. A U.S. Embassy statement issued this week said Washington remained "committed to a responsible drawdown of forces in close coordination with the government of Iraq."

Still, the mood on the streets suggested that many Iraqis remain unconvinced. Vendors closed their shops as the crowds swelled, and Iraqi army units sealed off approaches to the fortified Green Zone, where the parliament and government offices are located.

**Scenes From the Square**

For hours, the crowd surged through the boulevards, waving Iraqi flags and portraits of al-Sadr. Some demonstrators knelt in prayer on prayer rugs spread across the pavement before resuming their chants. Others carried mock coffins draped in American flags, a symbolic funeral for what they called the occupation.

"My brother died in the fighting. My cousin is in prison," said Umm Hassan, a woman in a black abaya who declined to give her full name. "For what? So they can promise to leave in three years? We have heard promises before."

Not all Iraqis share the Sadrists' rejection of the deal. In interviews away from the rally, some residents expressed cautious relief that a fixed departure date was finally on the table.

"At least now there is a date. Before, there was nothing," said Firas Abdul-Karim, a shopkeeper in the mixed Karrada neighborhood. "I do not love the Americans, but I fear what happens if they leave before we are ready."

**What Comes Next**

The Iraqi parliament is expected to take up the agreement in the coming days, with a vote possibly before the end of the month. Passage is not assured; the pact requires broad support to reflect national consensus, and Sunni and Kurdish blocs have raised their own concerns and demands.

Should parliament fail to ratify the agreement before the mandate expires, Iraqi and American officials would confront the prospect of either an emergency extension of the U.N. authorization — politically unpalatable to Baghdad — or an uncertain legal status for U.S. operations.

For the demonstrators who filled Firdos Square on Friday, the message was unambiguous, whatever the parliamentary arithmetic.

"The mandate is ending, and the occupation must end with it," al-Fartousi said as the crowd around him roared. "This is our country. It is time for us to have it back."

*— With additional reporting from the Baghdad bureau.*

# Tens of Thousands Rally in Baghdad Against U.S.-Iraq Security Pact

**BAGHDAD** — Massive crowds surged through the Iraqi capital's central square on Friday as tens of thousands of demonstrators denounced a proposed security agreement that would govern the presence of American forces in Iraq, transforming a routine day of prayer into one of the largest displays of anti-occupation sentiment in months.

The protest, drawing supporters from across the country, targeted a draft accord negotiated between Baghdad and Washington that would set the terms for U.S. military operations after the United Nations mandate authorizing the foreign troop presence expires at the end of the year.

## Immunity Provisions Draw Fierce Opposition

At the heart of the demonstrators' anger lies the question of legal immunity for American troops and private contractors. Under the terms being debated, U.S. personnel would retain significant protection from prosecution in Iraqi courts—a provision that critics describe as an affront to national sovereignty.

"We reject any agreement that places foreign soldiers above our laws," said one speaker addressing the crowd from a makeshift platform. "How can we call ourselves a free nation when those who kill our people cannot be judged by our courts?"

The immunity issue has proven especially contentious in the wake of incidents involving contractors and the deaths of Iraqi civilians. Negotiators on both sides have reportedly wrestled over language that would allow Iraqi jurisdiction in certain cases—particularly serious crimes committed off-duty and off-base—while preserving broad protections favored by the Pentagon.

## Demands for a Firm Withdrawal Timeline

Demonstrators also pressed for a clear and binding timetable for the departure of American forces. Many held banners calling for the immediate end of the occupation, while others demanded guarantees that any pullout deadline could not be extended or renegotiated behind closed doors.

The draft agreement under discussion reportedly envisions a phased withdrawal of combat forces from Iraqi cities and towns, followed by a broader departure over the following years. But protesters expressed deep skepticism that Washington would honor such commitments without external pressure.

"They speak of dates, but we have heard promises before," an elderly participant said. "We want them gone from our streets, our cities, and our country."

## Speeches Denounce Bush and the Occupation

The rally featured a series of impassioned addresses, many singling out U.S. President George Bush for direct criticism. Speakers accused the American administration of prolonging the occupation under the guise of security cooperation and of seeking to entrench long-term influence over Iraq's affairs.

Effigies and burning flags punctuated the gathering as chants echoed across the square, denouncing the American military presence and calling for national independence. Clerics aligned with the protest movement had urged followers in the preceding days to turn out in force, framing the demonstration as a peaceful expression of popular will.

"This is the voice of the Iraqi people," one prominent speaker declared. "We say to Bush and his government: leave our land. We do not want your bases, your soldiers, or your agreements that chain us."

## A Government Under Pressure

The scale of the protest underscored the political difficulties facing Iraqi leaders as they weigh the agreement. The government has sought to portray the accord as a means of restoring full sovereignty and ending the international mandate, while opponents view it as a mechanism to legitimize an extended American footprint.

Officials have insisted that no final deal has been signed and that Iraqi negotiators are pressing for terms that protect national interests, including firm withdrawal dates and limits on immunity. Still, the demonstration signaled that any agreement will face intense scrutiny in parliament and in the streets.

Security forces maintained a heavy but largely unobtrusive presence as the crowds gathered and later dispersed. The protest concluded without reports of significant violence, though organizers warned that further demonstrations would follow if their demands went unmet.

## What Comes Next

With the U.N. mandate set to expire, negotiators face a tightening window to finalize the framework governing U.S. operations. The coming weeks are expected to bring continued political maneuvering, as lawmakers debate the agreement's provisions and public pressure mounts.

For the tens of thousands who filled the square on Friday, the message was unmistakable: any pact that fails to guarantee accountability for foreign forces and a definite end to the occupation will meet with fierce resistance.
